summary: An informational RFC that recounts a discussion in the IETF DNS Working Group on load balancing, surveys other ways to provide or simulate it with the Domain Name System, and proposes a flexible approach for spreading load across servers.

plainLanguage.summary: The Domain Name System (DNS) is the Internet's directory, and it can also spread work. This memo explains how a DNS server can list several addresses for one name in an order that reflects how busy each computer is, so requests spread out instead of piling onto one machine. It does this without changing the DNS protocol.

questions: how can dns be used for load balancing
how can dns spread load across servers
what is a dns zone transfer agent
subtitle: Using DNS to spread traffic across several servers without changing the DNS.

tldr.problem: One name often stands for several servers that all do the same work, and the DNS has to hand out their addresses in a way that shares the work instead of loading one machine.
tldr.mechanism: The memo changes only the zone transfer, the step where a secondary name server refreshes its copy of a zone, so a program can sort the address records by load before the zone is served.
tldr.outcome: The DNS protocol itself is untouched, so servers already in place keep working. The cost is frequent refreshes, and the author measures how much processor time that costs.

today: RFC 1794 is an Informational memo from April 1995, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a trial that needed changes to the BIND name server, so it reads as a record of one workable approach rather than a specification that implementations are expected to follow.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1794 is an Informational memo that recounts a discussion in the IETF DNS Working Group about load balancing. It sets out three aims: to record what the working group tried, to survey other ways of providing or simulating load balancing in the DNS, and to present a flexible way of balancing many kinds of load.

Load balancing here means spreading requests across a set of machines that all do the same job. The DNS was designed to let several machines act as one, so that it did not matter which machine answered a query, provided the work was spread reasonably well across them.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is about using the Internet's directory to spread work. It reports what a working group tried, and proposes a way to keep the directory working the same way for everyone.

sections.title: How Load Balancing Was Tried Before
sections.content:
Around 1986, several schemes appeared as hacks to the BIND name server. The most widely distributed were the "Shuffle Address" modifications by Bryan Beecher and, possibly, Marshall Rose's round-robin code. Both simply rotated the address records; they did not look at the load on the target machines. Matt Madison of TGV changed that, using VMS facilities to read system loads and return address records ordered from least loaded to most loaded.

Two problems were seen with these schemes. Load was not really a factor in the round-robin versions, and the VMS-based one depended on facilities specific to that operating system. The "Shuffle Address" records also needed changes to the DNS specification, both in file syntax and in record processing, and that was judged a drawback rather than a general solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Early attempts simply shuffled the address list. They did not check how busy each machine was, and one of them needed the DNS specification to change.

sections.title: The Six Conditions Any Solution Must Meet
sections.content:
The DNS working group agreed that any solution had to meet six criteria: backwards compatibility with the existing DNS specification; information that changes frequently; multiple addresses sent out; correct interaction with other resource records; the ability to represent many types of load; and speed.

Several of these criteria shape the rest of the memo. Frequent changes allow real-time data, with five minutes thought of as a normal interval and changes as fast as every sixty seconds imaginable. Multiple addresses let a client's second choice appear when the first host has failed, because that address stays valid for the length of its time to live. Correct interaction covers auxiliary records such as MX, RP and TXT and reverse lookup information, so that mail handling keeps working. Representing many loads matters because the working group wanted to order addresses by round-trip time as well as by processor load, and a separate record type for each load would break the compatibility criterion.

The last criterion, speed, sets a limit. The time taken to calculate the ordering must not exceed the time to live of the information distributed, so records with a five-minute time to live cannot take six minutes to compute. Request processing must also carry on regardless of the state of any other processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The working group set six conditions for any answer. The two that shaped the design most were that the DNS had to keep working for everyone already using it, and that the answer had to be quick enough to be useful.

sections.title: A Model That Leaves the Protocol Alone
sections.content:
The solution keeps the DNS protocol unchanged and changes only the zone transfer. A zone transfer is how a secondary name server checks its primary and obtains a new copy of the zone when something has changed. No specification requires the secondary to receive its updates in any particular way, only that it check periodically and fetch a new copy when there have been changes.

A zone transfer agent, a program named in the configuration, therefore does the transfer. It can read the information from any source, such as a load average daemon or a round-robin sorter, and present it to the name server for distribution to clients. The DNS protocol does not guarantee ordering, but the ordering is predictable: information read twice in the same order is presented twice in the same order. Clients may reorder it themselves, which the memo treats as a local issue that a zone transfer agent can account for, since local mis-ordering is consistent.

Volatile zones need more care. Zone transfers are used only by secondaries, not by primary name servers, so a zone whose ordering changes every minute has to be refreshed often and handed out with a low time to live. With a very low refresh rate the primary and secondary must exchange data frequently, and they are usually far apart, so the memo calls that prohibitive. The longer the propagation time, the wider the window in which circumstances can change and the secondary's information goes stale. The memo concludes that passing volatile information to a secondary is of little use, and that secondaries wanting accurate information should calculate the ordering themselves. For such a zone there is no primary, only a series of autonomous secondary agents.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix leaves DNS alone and changes only the copy step. A second DNS server can ask a program for its zone data, and that program can sort the addresses however it likes.

sections.title: The Trial in BIND
sections.content:
With help from Masataka Ohta, the author modified BIND so that a zone transfer program could be named for a particular domain, using the configuration line transfer <domain-name> <program-name>. The implementation defines a separate subdomain holding the volatile information, with a refresh rate of 300 and a minimum time to live of 300.

Every 300 seconds a program named doAxfer runs to do the zone transfer. It reads a template file and a list file, rotates the addresses in the list a random number of times, and substitutes them in order into the template to generate the zone file. It then exits with a value of 1, telling the name server that the transfer succeeded and that the file should be read in and distributed. The result is a host with several addresses, randomized every five minutes.

Two bugs in BIND hampered this. The first was that BIND treated any time to live under 300 seconds as "irrational" and substituted 300, which greatly hampers volatile zones; at the fastest, a zero time to live would be used once and then thrown away. The second was that BIND treated any zone refresh rate under 15 minutes as equally irrational, and a 15-minute refresh is unacceptable for this application. The workaround sets both hard-coded values to 60 seconds, which is long enough to avoid residual bugs with small timers and short enough for fast subzones to be of use. This version of BIND was in release at Rutgers University, running both fast and normal zones.
sections.plainLanguage: The trial used a patched DNS server with one extra line of configuration naming the program to run. That program shuffled the addresses and wrote out the new zone file every five minutes.

sections.title: What the Refreshes Cost
sections.content:
Testing was done on a Sun Sparc-2 used as a normal workstation, with no resolvers using the name server. A configuration with no fast subzones accrued 11 CPU seconds in 24 hours. A configuration with one fast zone, six address records, refreshed every 300 seconds accrued 1 minute 4 seconds of CPU time. The same configuration refreshed every 60 seconds accrued 5 minutes and 38 seconds.

The processor load was linear to the frequency of the refresh. The 60-second configuration used about five times as much CPU time as the 300-second configuration, and the memo notes that overall CPU use would be linear to the number of zones and the refresh frequency. All of this was measured with a shell script that always indicated that a zone update was necessary; a more intelligent program would notice when reordering was unnecessary and avoid the periodic reloads.
sections.plainLanguage: Refreshing the zone every minute used about five times more processor time than refreshing it every five minutes. A faster answer therefore costs more, and administrators have to choose a point on that curve.

viz.caption: THE SIX CONDITIONS AGREED BY THE DNS WORKING GROUP

items.title: Backwards compatibility
items.text: The DNS as it already exists must keep working.

items.title: Frequent updates
items.text: The information changes often, so load can be followed closely.

items.title: Multiple addresses
items.text: Several addresses are sent out, so a second choice exists if a host fails.

items.title: Correct record interaction
items.text: MX, RP and TXT records and reverse lookups must keep working.

items.title: Many kinds of load
items.text: Any measure can be used, from processor load to round-trip time.

items.title: Speed
items.text: The order must be worked out faster than the time to live of the data.

messages.note: The program reads load information and returns the zone sorted.

messages.note: The addresses come back in the order the agent chose.
